title: NSW Coalition promises to protect jobs amid AI push
full_text:
The NSW Coalition will legislate that no key workers on the state’s frontline will lose their jobs due to increased use of artificial intelligence in the public sector, despite a pledge to aggressively ramp up use of the technology to drive efficiencies in government departments if it wins the next election.
Agencies in NSW will also be required to annually identify five examples of where AI can improve processes, and an AI productivity dividend will also be established, as part of the state opposition’s policy platform on the technology, to be revealed on Monday.
Cost savings generated by AI use will contribute to an agency’s efficiency dividend, while departments will also be given clear key performance indicators, aided by AI, that they must hit.
The opposition will write into law that frontline jobs for public sector workers, including nurses, police officers, teachers and social workers, would be protected from AI-related job losses, as they attempt to woo voters with a mantra that new efficiencies driven by technology won’t result in widespread job cuts for public servants.
The state Coalition’s AI platform will be revealed in a speech to the business sector by opposition digital and AI spokesman James Griffin on Monday.
Mr Griffin will reveal that if the Coalition wins the election next year, each new minister will be asked to identify within 90 days three opportunities within their portfolio where AI can deliver measurable outcomes.
Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said a newly established minister for artificial intelligence would be responsible for driving the changes.
“Our frontline workers are the backbone of NSW, and under a government I lead AI will be used to support them, not replace them,” Ms Sloane said.
“There is a huge opportunity through the use of AI to lift productivity across government by reducing paperwork, speeding up decision-making and giving frontline workers more time to do what the community relies on them for.”
The announcement of the NSW Coalition’s full AI policy builds on Mr Griffin revealing this year that the party would target overseas investment in data centres, by pitching NSW as a safe haven for the governments of Pacific neighbours to store their digital information.
Under its AI platform the NSW Coalition would also establish a state AI Solutions Fund that would include a co-investment mechanism between the government, the AI and data centre sector and university researchers, which would fund public-interest AI development.
“NSW should be leading the Asia-Pacific region in responsible use of AI, attracting investment and creating jobs while also ensuring a benefit to the community,” Mr Griffin said.
“We want to bring together government, universities and industry to solve real problems, from improving disaster response to better congestion management on our roads to get people home quicker.”
AI was discussed repeatedly at Labor’s national conference in Adelaide that ended on Saturday, with motions put forward including the possibility of workers getting more annual leave due to productivity gains from the technology.
The Albanese government also announced this month it would legislate “Australian standards for AI”, with that framework to be developed by a new AI section set up in the Prime Minister’s office.
The NSW government became the first state in the country to legislate against what it claimed were the risks arising from AI use in workplaces, with the new laws aimed at protecting workers from new digital systems that could place “excessive or unreasonable workloads for workers at work”.
The legislation also restricted AI being used to develop “excessive or unreasonable metrics to assess and track the performance of workers at work”.
